topic.name: Some Reactions of the Halide Ions

parts.problem_md:
Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to separate solid samples of sodium chloride and sodium bromide. In both reactions, steamy fumes are observed. However, in the reaction with sodium bromide, a brown gas is also produced.

Which statement correctly explains these observations?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium chloride, it acts only as an acid, producing hydrogen chloride gas observed as steamy fumes.
- Br<sup>-</sup> ions are stronger reducing agents than Cl<sup>-</sup> ions because reducing power of halide ions increases down Group 17.
- When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium bromide, the Br<sup>-</sup> ions reduce the sulfuric acid, producing bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>) observed as a brown gas, along with SO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O.

**A** is incorrect as option A describes an acid oxide reacting with sodium hydroxide, which is unrelated to the reactions described.

**C** is incorrect as Br<sup>-</sup> ions are oxidised to bromine in this reaction, not reduced. Br<sup>-</sup> loses electrons and its oxidation state increases from −1 to 0.

**D** is incorrect as sulfuric acid acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid (proton donor) when producing the steamy fumes of hydrogen halide, not as a base.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: It forms an acidic oxide that reacts with aqueous NaOH to form a salt.

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Br<sup>-</sup> ions are stronger reducing agents than Cl<sup>-</sup> ions.

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: Br<sup>-</sup> ions are more easily reduced to bromine than Cl<sup>-</sup> ions.

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: Sulfuric acid acts as a Brønsted–Lowry base in the reaction that produces steamy fumes.

parts.problem_md:
**Q** is a salt of one of the Group 17 elements chlorine, bromine, iodine, or astatine.

The reaction scheme shows a series of reactions using a solution of **Q** as the starting reagent.

**Q** (aq) `-> from AgNO _ 3 ( aq ) to HNO _ 3 ( aq ) of` precipitate $\xrightarrow{excess \text{dilute} NH_{3} ( \text{aq} )}$ colourless solution  $\xrightarrow{excess \text{dilute} HNO_{3} ( \text{aq} )}$ precipitate

What could **Q** be?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Adding acidified silver nitrate to a halide solution gives precipitates of different colours:

  - Cl<sup>-</sup> forms white AgCl
  - Br<sup>-</sup> forms cream AgBr
  - I<sup>-</sup> forms yellow AgI
  - At<sup>-</sup> forms yellow AgAt
- Only AgCl dissolves in excess dilute aqueous ammonia to give a colourless solution.
- The colourless solution reforms a precipitate on addition of excess dilute nitric acid, confirming the halide ion present is Cl<sup>-</sup>.

**B** is incorrect as sodium bromide gives a cream precipitate with acidified silver nitrate that remains insoluble in excess dilute aqueous ammonia.

**C** is incorrect as potassium iodide gives a yellow precipitate with acidified silver nitrate that remains insoluble in excess dilute aqueous ammonia.

**D** is incorrect as potassium astatide gives a yellow precipitate with acidified silver nitrate that remains insoluble in excess dilute aqueous ammonia.

choices.label: A

choices.text_md: Sodium bromide

choices.text_md: Potassium iodide

parts.problem_md: Which statement explains why the oxidising power of the halogens decreases down Group 17?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Down Group 17, the atomic radius increases as extra principal quantum shells are added.
- The outer shell is further from the nucleus and experiences greater shielding from inner electrons.
- An incoming electron therefore experiences less electrostatic attraction from the nucleus.
- The halogens' ability to attract and gain an electron (their oxidising power) decreases down the group.

**B** is incorrect as atomic radius increases down the group, not decreases.

**C** is incorrect as donating an electron describes oxidation, not reduction. This statement describes increasing reducing power, not decreasing oxidising power.

**D** is incorrect as electronegativity decreases down the group.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: Shielding increases down the group, making it more difficult to attract an incoming electron

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Atomic radius decreases down the group

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: Shielding increases down the group, making it easier to donate an electron

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: The halogens become more electronegative down the group

parts.problem_md:
Two students, R and S, were asked to draw bar charts to represent how some properties of the halogens and their compounds differ in magnitude. Their diagrams are shown.

![Two bar charts drawn by students R and S showing properties of halogens and their compounds. Student R's chart shows the enthalpy change for halogen reactions with hydrogen, with bar heights decreasing from Cl to Br to I indicating less exothermic reactions going down the group. Student S's chart shows the solubility of silver halides in ammonia, with bar heights increasing from AgCl to AgBr to AgI.](assets/001-two-bar-charts-drawn-by-students-r-and-s-showing.png)

Which of the students' diagrams is correct?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Student R's bar chart shows the enthalpy change for X<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → 2HX becoming less exothermic going down Group 17.
- This is correct as H–X bond strength decreases down the group, so less energy is released in the reaction.

**A** is incorrect as Student S's bar chart shows the wrong trend for the solubility of silver halides in ammonia. Solubility decreases down the group (AgCl dissolves in dilute ammonia, AgBr and AgI remain insoluble), not increases.

**C** is incorrect as only Student R's bar chart is correct. Student S's chart shows the wrong solubility trend for silver halides in ammonia.

**D** is incorrect as Student R's bar chart correctly shows the enthalpy change for X<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub> → 2HX becoming less exothermic going down Group 17.

parts.problem_md:
Solid potassium halides react with concentrated sulfuric acid, according to the following equations.

Reaction 1:     2KCl + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2HCl

Reaction 2:     2KBr + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + SO<sub>2</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

Reaction 3:     8KI + 5H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → 4K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>S + 4I<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

What is the largest change in the oxidation number of sulfur in each reaction?

|   | **Reaction 1** | **Reaction 2** | **Reaction 3** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 0 | 0 | 4 |
| **B** | 0 | 2 | 4 |
| **C** | 0 | 2 | 8 |
| **D** | 0 | 4 | 8 |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- In H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, the oxidation number of sulfur is +6 (H = +1, O = −2).
- In reaction 1, the only sulfur-containing product is K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, where sulfur is also +6, so the change is 0.
- In reaction 2, sulfur is reduced from +6 in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to +4 in SO<sub>2</sub>, so the largest change is 2.
- In reaction 3, sulfur is reduced from +6 in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to −2 in H<sub>2</sub>S, so the largest change is 6 − (−2) = 8.

**A** is incorrect as it gives 4 for reaction 3, which is the final oxidation state of sulfur in SO<sub>2</sub>, not the change in oxidation state from H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.

**B** is incorrect as it gives 4 for reaction 3, confusing the final oxidation state of sulfur in SO<sub>2</sub> (+4) with the change in oxidation state to H<sub>2</sub>S, which is 8.

**D** is incorrect as it gives 4 for reaction 2. The change from +6 in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to +4 in SO<sub>2</sub> is 2, not 4.

parts.problem_md:
The following two experiments are carried out with anhydrous potassium chloride.

**Experiment 1:** Aqueous silver nitrate is added to an aqueous solution of potassium chloride, followed by an excess of aqueous ammonia - observation **X**.

**Experiment 2:** Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid potassium chloride, and the fumes produced are bubbled into aqueous potassium iodide solution - observation **Y**.

Which row correctly identifies observations **X** and **Y**?

|   | **X** | **Y** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Colourless solution | Brown solution |
| **B** | Colourless solution | Colourless solution |
| **C** | White precipitate | Brown solution |
| **D** | White precipitate | Colourless solution |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- **Experiment 1 (Observation X):**

  - AgNO<sub>3</sub> reacts with Cl<sup>-</sup> ions to form a white precipitate of AgCl.
  - When aqueous ammonia is added, AgCl dissolves to form a soluble diamminesilver(I) complex, leaving a colourless solution

- **Experiment 2 (Observation Y):**

  - Concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid potassium chloride in an acid-base reaction:

KCl (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → KHSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + HCl (g)

- The HCl fumes dissolve in the aqueous potassium iodide to form hydrochloric acid
- HCl is not an oxidising agent and cannot remove electrons from iodide ions (I<sup>-</sup>), so no displacement reaction occurs and the solution remains colourless

**A** and **C** are incorrect as they suggest a brown solution for observation Y. You might assume that 'chloride fumes' entering a potassium iodide solution would displace iodide to form brown iodine, but this requires the elemental halogen (Cl<sub>2</sub>). HCl is an acid, not an oxidising agent, and does not displace I<sup>-</sup>

**C** and **D** are incorrect as they show a white precipitate for observation X. AgCl does form initially, but it dissolves completely in aqueous ammonia, leaving a colourless solution

parts.problem_md:
Element 85, astatine, is a halogen. When concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium astatide, the products are astatine, hydrogen astatide, hydrogen sulfide and sodium sulfate.

Which product is formed by the oxidation of one of the constituents of sodium astatide?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium astatide, it acts as both an acid and an oxidising agent.
- The astatide ion (At<sup>-</sup>) is oxidised to elemental astatine (At<sub>2</sub>):

2At<sup>-</sup> → At<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup>

- Astatine (At<sub>2</sub>) is therefore the product formed by oxidation of At<sup>-</sup>, a constituent of sodium astatide.

**A** is incorrect as sodium sulfate is produced in the acid-base reaction between NaAt and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Na<sup>+</sup> is not oxidised.

**B** is incorrect as hydrogen sulfide is formed when sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is reduced from +6 to −2. It is a reduction product of sulfuric acid, not an oxidation product of a constituent of NaAt.

**C** is incorrect as hydrogen astatide is formed in the acid-base step (At<sup>-</sup> + H<sup>+</sup> → HAt). The At<sup>-</sup> ion is not oxidised in this step.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: Sodium sulfate

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Hydrogen sulfide

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: Hydrogen astatide

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: Astatine

parts.problem_md:
A powder is known to be either a single sodium halide or a mixture of two different sodium halides.

An aqueous solution of the powder produces a pale yellow precipitate when tested with acidified aqueous silver nitrate. When concentrated aqueous ammonia is added, the precipitate partially dissolves, leaving a darker yellow precipitate.

What does the powder contain?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Adding acidified silver nitrate to a mixture of chloride and iodide ions produces white AgCl and yellow AgI.

  - The combined precipitate appears pale yellow.
- When concentrated aqueous ammonia is added, AgCl dissolves to form a soluble complex but AgI remains completely insoluble.
- The removal of the white AgCl leaves only the yellow AgI, making the remaining precipitate appear a darker yellow.

**A** is incorrect as pure sodium iodide would give a yellow precipitate of AgI that does not dissolve at all when concentrated aqueous ammonia is added.

**B** is incorrect as pure sodium bromide would give a cream precipitate of AgBr, not a pale yellow one. AgBr dissolves completely in concentrated aqueous ammonia, so no solid would remain.

**C** is incorrect as a mixture of sodium chloride and sodium bromide would give a pale to cream precipitate. Both AgCl and AgBr dissolve completely in concentrated aqueous ammonia, so the entire precipitate would dissolve rather than partially.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: Sodium iodide only

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Sodium bromide only

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: A mixture of sodium chloride and sodium bromide

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: A mixture of sodium chloride and sodium iodide

parts.problem_md:
A student observed the reactions when solid sodium bromide and solid sodium fluoride were each reacted separately with concentrated sulfuric acid and concentrated phosphoric acid. The observations are recorded in the table below.

|   | **Sodium bromide** | **Sodium fluoride** |
|---|---|---|
| **Concentrated H**<sub>**2**</sub>**SO**<sub>**4**</sub> | Steamy fumes and brown vapour | Colourless acidic gas formed |
| **Concentrated H**<sub>**3**</sub>**PO**<sub>**4**</sub> | Colourless acidic gas formed | Colourless acidic gas formed |

Which deduction can be made from these observations?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Concentrated sulfuric acid can act both as an acid and as an oxidising agent
- When it acts as an acid, it produces the hydrogen halide; all halide salts react in this way
- The reactions of solid sodium fluoride with both acids are acid-base reactions only
- The reaction of solid sodium bromide with concentrated phosphoric acid is also an acid-base reaction only
- When concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium bromide:

  - Bromide ions are strong enough reducing agents to reduce H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
  - Bromide ions are oxidised to bromine:

2HBr (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → Br<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

- The brown vapour of bromine confirms that concentrated sulfuric acid is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine

**A** is incorrect as concentrated phosphoric acid only acts as an acid in these reactions. It is not an oxidising agent and is therefore a weaker oxidising agent than bromine

**B** is incorrect as concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises bromide ions but concentrated phosphoric acid does not. Concentrated sulfuric acid is therefore the stronger oxidising agent

**C** is incorrect as concentrated sulfuric acid is not a strong enough oxidising agent to oxidise fluoride ions. No redox reaction occurs with sodium fluoride under these conditions

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: Concentrated phosphoric acid is a stronger oxidising agent than concentrated sulfuric acid.

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Concentrated phosphoric acid is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine.

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: Concentrated sulfuric acid is a stronger oxidising agent than fluorine.

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: Concentrated sulfuric acid is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine.

parts.problem_md: Which observations are made when solid sodium bromide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Concentrated sulfuric acid acts as an acid, reacting with solid sodium bromide to produce hydrogen bromide gas:

NaBr (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → NaHSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + HBr (g)

- Bromide ions are strong enough reducing agents to also reduce the sulfuric acid, producing bromine gas and sulfur dioxide:

2HBr (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → Br<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

- Bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>) is observed as a red-brown gas and SO<sub>2</sub> has a pungent, choking odour.

**A** is incorrect as steamy fumes only is the observation for solid sodium chloride reacting with concentrated sulfuric acid. The chloride ion is not a strong enough reducing agent to reduce the sulfuric acid.

**B** is incorrect as a yellow solid of sulfur is only produced in the reaction with sodium iodide, not sodium bromide. The iodide ion is a stronger reducing agent than bromide.

**C** is incorrect as a yellow solid indicates iodide chemistry, not bromide chemistry.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: Steamy fumes only

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Red-brown gas and yellow solid produced

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: Yellow solid produced

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: Red-brown gas and pungent odour

parts.problem_md: Which anion forms a white precipitate when tested with acidified aqueous silver nitrate?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Chloride ions react with acidified aqueous silver nitrate to form a white precipitate of silver chloride:

Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgCl (s)

**A** is incorrect as carbonate ions are tested with dilute acid, which produces effervescence but no white precipitate with silver nitrate.

**B** is incorrect as sulfate ions are tested with acidified barium chloride solution, producing a white precipitate of barium sulfate (BaSO<sub>4</sub>).

**C** is incorrect as the acid removes any hydroxide ions from solution before silver nitrate is added. Even without acid, silver ions would react with hydroxide ions to form brown silver oxide (Ag<sub>2</sub>O), not a white precipitate.

parts.problem_md:
Astatine is the element below iodine in Group 17 of the Periodic Table.

Which statement about astatine is most likely to be correct?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Down Group 17, the reducing power of the halide ions increases as atomic radius increases and shielding increases, making it easier for the ion to lose an electron.
- The astatide ion (At<sup>-</sup>) is therefore a very strong reducing agent.
- When solid sodium astatide reacts with hot concentrated sulfuric acid, the astatide ion reduces the H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and is itself oxidised to form elemental astatine (At<sub>2</sub>).

**A** is incorrect as the solubility of silver halides in ammonia decreases down the group. AgAt will be even less soluble than AgI, which is insoluble in both dilute and concentrated aqueous ammonia.

**C** is incorrect as astatine is a weaker oxidising agent than chlorine. A halogen can only displace a halide ion of a weaker oxidising agent, so no reaction would take place.

**D** is incorrect as astatide ions are strong enough reducing agents to also reduce sulfuric acid, so the reaction produces H<sub>2</sub>S and At<sub>2</sub> alongside other products, not just hydrogen astatide fumes.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: Silver astatide reacts with dilute aqueous ammonia in excess to form a solution of a soluble complex.

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Solid sodium astatide and hot concentrated sulfuric acid react to form astatine.

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: Astatine and aqueous potassium chloride react to form aqueous potassium astatide and chlorine.

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: Solid potassium astatide and concentrated sulfuric acid react to produce white fumes of hydrogen astatide only.

parts.problem_md: Which compounds are produced when solid potassium bromide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Concentrated sulfuric acid acts as an acid, donating a proton to the bromide ion to produce potassium hydrogensulfate and hydrogen bromide:

KBr (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → KHSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + HBr (g)

- Bromide ions are strong enough reducing agents to also reduce the sulfuric acid, producing bromine gas and sulfur dioxide:

2HBr (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → Br<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

- The complete set of products from both reactions is potassium hydrogensulfate, hydrogen bromide, bromine, sulfur dioxide and water.

**B** is incorrect as it omits sulfur dioxide, which is formed when bromide ions reduce the sulfuric acid.

**C** is incorrect as it omits both sulfur dioxide and water, which are produced in the redox step.

**D** is incorrect as it only lists the acid-base products. Bromide ions are strong enough reducing agents to also reduce sulfuric acid, producing bromine, sulfur dioxide and water.

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: Potassium hydrogen sulfate, hydrogen bromide, bromine, water and sulfur dioxide

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: Potassium hydrogen sulfate, hydrogen bromide, bromine and water

choices.label: C
choices.text_md: Potassium hydrogen sulfate, hydrogen bromide and bromine

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: Potassium hydrogen sulfate and hydrogen bromide

parts.problem_md:
Which row correctly identifies the chemical test and observation for an iodide ion?

|   | **Chemical test** | **Observation** |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Acidified aqueous silver nitrate | Yellow precipitate insoluble in concentrated aqueous ammonia |
| **B** | Acidified barium chloride | White precipitate insoluble in hydrochloric acid |
| **C** | Acidified potassium nitrate | Yellow precipitate insoluble in concentrated aqueous ammonia |
| **D** | Bromine water | Brown solution changes to colourless solution |
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Acidified aqueous silver nitrate reacts with iodide ions to form a yellow precipitate of silver iodide (AgI).
- AgI is the least soluble of the silver halides and remains insoluble in both dilute and concentrated aqueous ammonia.

**B** is incorrect as acidified barium chloride is the test for sulfate ions, which produces a white precipitate of barium sulfate (BaSO<sub>4</sub>).

**C** is incorrect as potassium nitrate is not used to test for halide ions. All potassium and nitrate salts are soluble, so no precipitate would form.

**D** is incorrect as bromine water is the test for carbon-carbon double bonds in alkenes. Adding bromine water to iodide ions would cause bromine to oxidise the iodide, producing more brown iodine rather than a colourless solution.

parts.problem_md: Construct an ionic equation, including state symbols, to show the reaction between aqueous silver nitrate, AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq), and aqueous sodium iodide, NaI (aq).
parts.solution_md:
The ionic equation for the reaction between aqueous silver nitrate and aqueous sodium iodide is:

Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + I<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgI (s)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct ionic equation: Ag<sup>+</sup> + I<sup>-</sup> → AgI
> 
> 1 mark for correct state symbols: (aq), (aq), (s)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When silver nitrate solution is added to a solution containing halide ions, a precipitate forms. The state symbol for the precipitate is always (s).
> 
> The spectator ions (Na<sup>+</sup> and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup>) are omitted from ionic equations as they do not participate in the reaction.
> 
> Fluoride ions do not produce a precipitate as silver fluoride, AgF, is soluble in water.
> 
> All nitrate salts are soluble in water.

parts.problem_md:
Sodium iodide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid via the following equation.

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) + NaI (s) → HI (g) + NaHSO<sub>4</sub> (s)

Hydrogen iodide reacts further with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to produce a yellow solid, a purple vapour, and a gas with a smell of rotten eggs.

i) Identify the three products responsible for these observations.

yellow solid ........................................

smell of rotten eggs ........................................

purple vapour ........................................

[3]

ii) Construct an equation for the reaction of HI with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to form the yellow solid and the purple vapour. Include state symbols in your answer.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The three products responsible for the observations are:
> 
> - Yellow solid: sulfur / S **[1 mark]**
> - Smell of rotten eggs: hydrogen sulfide / H<sub>2</sub>S **[1 mark]**
> - Purple vapour: iodine / I<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), the concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises hydrogen iodide. The sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> starts at oxidation state +6. It can be reduced to S (yellow solid, oxidation state 0) or further to H<sub>2</sub>S (rotten egg smell, oxidation state -2). Iodine is produced as a purple vapour.
> 
> There is a further product in this reaction: sulfur dioxide gas.

ii) The equation for the reaction of HI with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to form the yellow solid and the purple vapour is:

6HI (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → 3I<sub>2</sub> (g) + S (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants and products
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing and state symbols

> **[exam-tip]**
> To balance this equation, start with S (already balanced), then balance O using H<sub>2</sub>O, then work back to balance H and finally I:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → S (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> - 6HI (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → 3I<sub>2</sub> (g) + S (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

parts.problem_md:
When sodium bromide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid, bromine and sulfur dioxide are formed.

Construct an ionic half-equation for the oxidation of bromide ions to bromine.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The ionic half-equation for the oxidation of bromide ions to bromine is:
> 
> - 2Br<sup>-</sup> → Br<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When sodium bromide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid, hydrogen bromide is produced initially:
> 
> NaBr (s) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → NaHSO<sub>4</sub> (s) + HBr (g)
> 
> This is followed by the oxidation of HBr, with sulfuric acid acting as the oxidising agent and being reduced to sulfur dioxide:
> 
> 2HBr (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) → Br<sub>2</sub> (g) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> 
> Iodide ions are stronger reducing agents than bromide ions and can reduce the sulfur in sulfuric acid further, all the way to H<sub>2</sub>S. This is because the larger iodide ion has more electron shells, so its outermost electrons are further from the nucleus and held less tightly, making them easier to donate.

parts.problem_md:
This question is about the redox reactions of halide ions.

Chlorine can displace iodine from potassium iodide.

i) Construct the balanced equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Construct the ionic equation for this reaction.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The balanced equation for the displacement of iodine by chlorine is:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KI → 2KCl + I<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The ionic equation for this reaction is:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2I<sup>-</sup> → 2Cl<sup>-</sup> + I<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When constructing the ionic equation, the spectator ion K<sup>+</sup> cancels out. Remember to include the balancing numbers for the halide ions.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

This question is about the redox reactions of halide ions.

Chlorine can displace iodine from potassium iodide.

i) Construct the balanced equation for this reaction.

ii) Construct the ionic equation for this reaction.

i) The balanced equation for the displacement of iodine by chlorine is:

- Cl~2~ + 2KI → 2KCl + I~2~

ii) The ionic equation for this reaction is:

- Cl~2~ + 2I^-^ → 2Cl^-^ + I~2~

Using oxidation numbers, explain how iodide ions act as a reducing agent in this reaction.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Iodide ions act as a reducing agent in this reaction:
> 
> - Reducing agents decrease the oxidation number of another atom
> - Iodide ions / I<sup>-</sup> cause the oxidation number of Cl to decrease from 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) to −1 (in Cl<sup>-</sup>)
> 
> **OR**
> 
> - The reducing agent is the substance that gets oxidised
> - The oxidation number of I increases from −1 (in I<sup>-</sup>) to 0 (in I<sub>2</sub>), so I is oxidised
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> References to electrons instead of oxidation numbers are not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question asks for an explanation in terms of oxidation numbers. Any reference to electron transfer instead of oxidation number changes will not be credited.
> 
> A reducing agent can be identified in two ways: by identifying which species causes a decrease in another’s oxidation number (Cl in Cl<sub>2</sub> goes from 0 to −1), or by identifying which species is itself oxidised (I goes from −1 to 0 in I<sub>2</sub>).

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

This question is about the redox reactions of halide ions.

Chlorine can displace iodine from potassium iodide.

i) Construct the balanced equation for this reaction.

The balanced equation for the displacement of iodine by chlorine is:
- Cl~2~ + 2KI → 2KCl + I~2~

The ionic equation for this reaction is:
- Cl~2~ + 2I^-^ → 2Cl^-^ + I~2~

i) Chlorine also displaces bromine from potassium bromide but not as readily as it can displace iodine from potassium iodide.

Explain how you can use these results to determine which is the stronger reducing agent, bromide ions or iodide ions.

[2]

ii) Explain why the halide ions show this trend in reducing power.

[4]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) To determine which is the stronger reducing agent:
> 
> - A stronger reducing agent will donate electrons more readily **[1 mark]**
> - Iodide ions donate electrons more readily than bromide ions to chlorine, so iodide ions are the stronger reducing agent **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The trend in reducing power down Group 17 is explained by:
> 
> - Going down the group, the halide ions become larger / ionic radius increases **[1 mark]**
> - The outermost electrons are further from the nucleus
> **OR**
> The outer electrons experience greater shielding from inner electrons **[1 mark]**
> - There is less attraction between the outer electrons and the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> - The halide ions lose electrons more readily going down the group, so reducing power increases **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For part i), link the experimental observation directly to reducing ability, i.e. the halide ion that is displaced more readily by chlorine is the stronger reducing agent.
> 
> For part ii), the trend in reducing power down Group 17 is due to increasing ionic radius. More electron shells means more shielding, which weakens the attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electrons, making them more easily donated.

parts.problem_md:
Iodide ions can also act as a reducing agent to reduce Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions to Fe<sup>2+</sup>.

i) Construct the ionic equation for this reaction.

[2]

ii) Explain, in terms of electrons, how Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions act as an oxidising agent.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
i) The ionic equation for the reaction between iodide ions and Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions is:

2I<sup>-</sup> + 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2Fe<sup>2+</sup>

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct reactants and products
> 
> 1 mark for correct balancing

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions act as an oxidising agent because:
> 
> - Oxidising agents accept electrons from another species **[1 mark]**
> - Fe<sup>3+</sup> accepts an electron from I<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To construct the ionic equation, write the two half-equations:
> 
> - Oxidation: 2I<sup>-</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup>
> - Reduction: Fe<sup>3+</sup> + e<sup>-</sup> → Fe<sup>2+</sup>
> 
> Multiply the iron half-equation by 2 so both contain 2e<sup>-</sup>, then cancel the electrons:
> 
> - 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup> → 2Fe<sup>2+</sup>
> - 2I<sup>-</sup> + 2Fe<sup>3+</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2Fe<sup>2+</sup>
> 
> For part ii), the question asks for an explanation in terms of electrons only. References to oxidation numbers will not be credited.

parts.problem_md:
Three solutions of sodium salts are labelled **X**, **Y** and **Z**. The results of tests carried out on each solution are shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Unknown** | **Test** | **Result** |
|---|---|---|
| **X** | Added acidified silver nitrate solution. Then added concentrated ammonia solution. | Yellow precipitate formed. Precipitate remained. |
| **Y** | Added acidified barium chloride solution. | White precipitate formed. |
| **Z** | Added acidified silver nitrate solution. Then added concentrated ammonia solution. | Cream precipitate formed. Precipitate dissolved. |

Identify **X**, **Y** and **Z** and construct ionic equations, including state symbols, to demonstrate the key reaction in each test.

- **X**:
- ionic equation:

[2]

- **Y**:
- ionic equation:

[2]

- **Z**:
- ionic equation:

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The identity of **X** and its ionic equation are:
> 
> - X = sodium iodide / NaI **[1 mark]**
> - Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + I<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgI (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The identity of **Y** and its ionic equation are:
> 
> - Y = sodium sulfate / Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - Ba<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) → BaSO<sub>4</sub> (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The identity of **Z** and its ionic equation are:
> 
> - Z = sodium bromide / NaBr **[1 mark]**
> - Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Br<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgBr (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> If chemical formulae are given, they must be correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> All ionic precipitation equations require state symbols: (aq) for dissolved ions and (s) for the precipitate.
> 
> For the silver nitrate test, the colour of the precipitate identifies the halide:
> 
> - Yellow precipitate = iodide (I<sup>-</sup>)
> - Cream precipitate = bromide (Br<sup>-</sup>)
> - White precipitate = chloride (Cl<sup>-</sup>)
> 
> The barium chloride test must be acidified (with dilute HCl) to be specific for sulfate ions. Acidification removes interfering anions such as sulfite and carbonate.

parts.problem_md:
The following statements are about oxidising ability in Group 17.

Statement **A**: The oxidising ability of the halide ions increases down the group.

Statement **B**: The oxidising ability of the halogen molecules increases down the group.

State whether Statement **A**, Statement **B** or neither is correct. Justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Assessing the two statements:
> 
> - Neither statement is correct **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidising ability involves the gain of electrons, and halide ions do not gain electrons
> **OR**
> Halide ions lose / donate electrons (so have reducing ability, not oxidising ability)
> **OR**
> Reducing ability of halide ions increases down the group
> **OR**
> It is the halogens (not halide ions) that gain electrons **[1 mark]**
> - Oxidising ability of the halogens decreases down the group
> **OR**
> Oxidising ability of the halogens increases up the group **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is important to distinguish between halogens (X<sub>2</sub>, diatomic molecules) and halide ions (X<sup>-</sup>, anions).
> 
> - Halogens gain electrons and act as oxidising agents. Oxidising ability decreases down Group 17.
> - Halide ions lose electrons and act as reducing agents. Reducing ability increases down Group 17.

parts.problem_md:
On gently heating, the compound KClO<sub>3</sub> reacts as shown in the equation.

4KClO<sub>3</sub> (s) → KCl (s) + 3KClO<sub>4</sub> (s)

This reaction is an example of disproportionation.

State what is meant by disproportionation and use oxidation numbers to show that disproportionation has taken place.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The meaning of disproportionation and evidence from oxidation numbers:
> 
> - Disproportionation is the simultaneous oxidation and reduction of the **same element** (in a single reaction) **[1 mark]**
> - Cl is oxidised from +5 (in KClO<sub>3</sub>) to +7 (in KClO<sub>4</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - Cl is reduced from +5 (in KClO<sub>3</sub>) to −1 (in KCl) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Disproportionation must involve the same element, not just the same compound. In this example, it is the chlorine atom that undergoes both oxidation (+5 to +7) and reduction (+5 to −1) simultaneously.

parts.problem_md:
Bromine is used to extract iodine from a solution containing iodide ions.

Explain why iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than bromine.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Iodine is a weaker oxidising agent than bromine because:
> 
> - Iodine has a larger atomic radius than bromine **[1 mark]**
> - Iodine has more electron shells, so there is greater shielding of the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> - There is weaker nuclear attraction on a gained electron (than in bromine) / iodine gains electrons less readily than bromine **[1 mark]**
> 
> The reverse argument (explaining why bromine is the stronger oxidising agent) is also accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Oxidising ability decreases down Group 17 because each successive element has a larger atomic radius and more electron shielding. This reduces the nuclear attraction on incoming electrons, making it harder to gain an electron.
> 
> Bromine is above iodine in Group 17, so it has a smaller radius, less shielding, and stronger nuclear attraction. This makes it a better oxidising agent.

parts.problem_md:
The equation for the reaction between solid potassium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid is:

2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (l) + 2KBr (s) → K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + Br<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Identify the **two** redox products and one possible observation for each.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The two redox products and a possible observation for each are:
> 
> - SO<sub>2</sub> / sulfur dioxide **[1 mark]**
> - Colourless gas evolved / colourless fumes **[1 mark]**
> - Br<sub>2</sub> / bromine **[1 mark]**
> - Brown / orange gas / vapour evolved **[1 mark]**
> 
> K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O are not accepted because they are not redox products

> **[exam-tip]**
> Only products that have undergone a change in oxidation state count as redox products. K<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O are not redox products.
> 
> The redox products are SO<sub>2</sub> (sulfur is reduced from +6 to +4) and Br<sub>2</sub> (bromine is oxidised from −1 to 0).
> 
> SO<sub>2</sub> is colourless but has a pungent smell. It can be confirmed by holding it near filter paper soaked in acidified potassium dichromate(VI) solution nearby, which changes colour from orange to green.

parts.problem_md: Explain why the reaction between solid potassium iodide and concentrated sulfuric acid produces hydrogen sulfide whereas the reaction between solid potassium bromide and concentrated sulfuric acid does not.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The iodide ion reduces H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to H<sub>2</sub>S, but the bromide ion cannot, because:
> 
> - I<sup>–</sup> / iodide ion is a stronger reducing agent than Br<sup>–</sup> / bromide ion **[1 mark]**
> - I<sup>–</sup> / iodide ion has a larger ionic radius / more electron shells / greater shielding than Br<sup>–</sup> / bromide ion **[1 mark]**
> - Outer electron(s) more easily removed / donated from I<sup>–</sup> than Br<sup>–</sup> / I<sup>–</sup> more readily donates electrons **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Reducing power increases down Group 17. Iodide ions are stronger reducing agents than bromide ions because they have more electron shells, which increases shielding and means the outermost electrons are further from the nucleus.
> 
> This makes the outermost electrons more easily donated. Iodide is therefore strong enough to reduce the sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> from an oxidation state of +6 to −2 in H<sub>2</sub>S. Bromide is not.

parts.problem_md: In aqueous solution, hydrogen fluoride is classified as a weak acid, whereas hydrogen chloride is classified as a strong acid. Explain this difference.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in acid strength is due to the relative H–X bond strengths:
> 
> - The H–F bond is stronger / shorter than the H–Cl bond **[1 mark]**
> - H–Cl bond breaks more readily / dissociates more fully, releasing more H<sup>+</sup> ions
> **OR**
> H–F bond does not break as easily, so fewer H<sup>+</sup> ions are released **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A strong acid fully dissociates in solution, releasing a high concentration of H<sup>+</sup> ions. A weak acid only partially dissociates, releasing far fewer H<sup>+</sup> ions.
> 
> HCl → H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq) (complete dissociation)
> 
> HF ⇌ H<sup>+</sup> (aq) + F<sup>–</sup> (aq) (partial dissociation)
> 
> Fluorine is the smallest halogen, so the H–F bond is the shortest and strongest of the hydrogen halides. This makes HF much less likely to dissociate completely, so it is classified as a weak acid.

parts.problem_md:
When solid NaCl reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid the only gas produced is HCl (g) and when solid NaBr reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid the gases produced are brown fumes of Br<sub>2</sub> (g) as well as HBr (g).

Explain the difference in the reactions of concentrated sulfuric acid with NaBr and with NaCl. Your answer should refer to the role of the sulfuric acid in each reaction.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in the reactions of concentrated sulfuric acid with NaBr and with NaCl is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> acts only as an acid with NaCl, producing HCl
> **OR**
> NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NaHSO<sub>4</sub> + HCl
> **OR**
> 2NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2HCl **[1 mark]**
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> also acts as an oxidising agent with NaBr, producing Br<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> Br<sup>-</sup> / NaBr acts as a reducing agent **[1 mark]**
> - Br<sup>-</sup> is a stronger reducing agent than Cl<sup>-</sup> / Br<sup>-</sup> is more easily oxidised than Cl<sup>-</sup>
> **OR**
> H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> can oxidise Br<sup>-</sup> but not Cl<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> With NaCl, the reaction is acid-base only: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> donates H<sup>+</sup> to Cl<sup>-</sup>, forming HCl. No oxidation or reduction occurs.
> 
> With NaBr, there is both an acid-base reaction (forming HBr) and a redox reaction: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> acts as an oxidising agent, accepting electrons from Br<sup>-</sup>. This occurs because Br<sup>-</sup> is a stronger reducing agent than Cl<sup>-</sup> and is more readily oxidised.
> 
> Reducing power of halide ions increases down Group 17: the larger the ion, the more easily it donates electrons.

parts.problem_md:
Solid sodium iodide, NaI (s), reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid to form purple fumes of I<sub>2</sub> (g), a yellow solid and hydrogen sulfide gas, H<sub>2</sub>S (g).

i) Construct the half-equation for the formation of the yellow solid.

[1]

ii) Construct the half-equation for the formation of iodine gas.

[1]

iii) Hence construct the full equation using your answers to parts **(b)(i)** and **(b)(ii)**.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The half-equation for the formation of the yellow solid (S) is:
> 
> - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 6H<sup>+</sup> + 6e<sup>-</sup> → S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The half-equation for the formation of iodine is:
> 
> - 2I<sup>-</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The full equation is:
> 
> - 6I<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 6H<sup>+</sup> → 3I<sub>2</sub> + S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To balance the half-equation for sulfur formation:
> 
> 1. Balance S atoms (already balanced)
> 2. Balance O atoms by adding H<sub>2</sub>O: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
> 3. Balance H atoms by adding H<sup>+</sup>: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 6H<sup>+</sup> → S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
> 4. Balance charge by adding e<sup>-</sup>: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 6H<sup>+</sup> + 6e<sup>-</sup> → S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> To construct the full equation, multiply the iodide half-equation by 3 so both contain 6e<sup>-</sup>:
> 
> - 6I<sup>-</sup> → 3I<sub>2</sub> + 6e<sup>-</sup>
> 
> Cancel the electrons: 6I<sup>-</sup> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 6H<sup>+</sup> → 3I<sub>2</sub> + S + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

parts.problem_md:
Chlorine reacts with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide solution.

i) Construct the equation for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Use oxidation numbers to explain why this is a disproportionation reaction.

[2]

iii) In terms of electrons, state the meaning of the term oxidising agent.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide is:
> 
> - 3Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + 6NaOH (aq) → 5NaCl (aq) + NaClO<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are not required
> 
> ii) This is a disproportionation reaction because:
> 
> - Chlorine is simultaneously oxidised and reduced / the same element is both oxidised and reduced **[1 mark]**
> - Cl oxidation state changes from 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) to +5 (in NaClO<sub>3</sub>)
> **AND**
> Cl oxidation state changes from 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) to −1 (in NaCl) **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The meaning of the term oxidising agent is:
> 
> - (A species that) gains electrons
> **OR**
> An electron acceptor **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You need to know the equations for the reaction of chlorine with both hot and cold sodium hydroxide:
> 
> - Cold NaOH  (forming sodium chlorate(I)):
> 
> Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2NaOH (aq) → NaCl (aq) + NaOCl (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> 
> - Hot NaOH (forming sodium chlorate(V)):
> 
> 3Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + 6NaOH (aq) → 5NaCl (aq) + NaClO<sub>3</sub> (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
> 
> For part ii), the oxidation state of Cl in NaClO<sub>3</sub>: Na (+1) and 3 × O (−2) = −6, so Cl = +5.
> 
> For part iii), oxidising agents gain electrons (they are reduced). Do not confuse with reducing agents, which lose electrons (they are oxidised).

parts.problem_md:
Chlorine is added to drinking water to ensure that it is safe to drink.

State a concern with adding chlorine to drinking water.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A valid concern with adding chlorine to drinking water is:
> 
> Any **one** from:
> 
> - Chlorine is potentially toxic if too concentrated
> - Some people find the taste unpleasant
> - Can react with organic compounds to produce harmful / toxic substances
> 
> **[1 mark]**

parts.problem_md:
Aqueous silver nitrate, AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq), is added to separate solutions of NaI and NaCl and precipitates form. An excess of aqueous ammonia is then added to both precipitates.

i) Complete Table 1.1 to state the colour and name of the precipitate formed in each reaction and the effect of the addition of an excess of aqueous ammonia to each of the precipitates formed.

**Table 1.1**

|   | **NaI (aq) + AgNO**<sub>3</sub>** (aq)** | **NaCl (aq) + AgNO**<sub>3</sub>** (aq)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Colour of precipitate** |   |   |
| **Name of precipitate** |   |   |
| **Effect of addition of an excess of aqueous ammonia to the precipitate** |   |   |

[3]

ii) Construct an ionic equation to show the reaction occurring when AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) is added to NaI (aq).

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) The completed Table 1.1 is:

|   | **NaI (aq) + AgNO**<sub>3</sub>** (aq)** | **NaCl (aq) + AgNO**<sub>3</sub>** (aq)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Colour of precipitate** | **Final answer:** **yellow** | **Final answer:** **white** |
| **Name of precipitate** | **Final answer:** **silver iodide** | **Final answer:** **silver chloride** |
| **Effect of addition of an excess of aqueous ammonia to the precipitate** | **Final answer:** **no (visible) change** | **Final answer:** **dissolves / soluble** |

**[3 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct colour and name of precipitate from NaI: yellow, silver iodide
> 
> 1 mark for correct colour and name of precipitate from NaCl: white, silver chloride
> 
> 1 mark for correct effects of aqueous ammonia: no change (AgI); dissolves to form a colourless solution (AgCl)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The ionic equation for the reaction when AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) is added to NaI (aq) is:
> 
> - Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + I<sup>-</sup> (aq) → AgI (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required for this precipitation reaction.

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must learn the tests for halide ions thoroughly. The colour of the silver halide precipitate and its solubility in aqueous ammonia are the key distinguishing observations:
> 
> - AgCl (white) dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia
> - AgBr (cream) dissolves only in concentrated aqueous ammonia
> - AgI (yellow) is insoluble in aqueous ammonia at any concentration
> 
> Include state symbols when writing ionic equations for precipitation reactions, even if not explicitly asked, as these may be required for the mark.

parts.problem_md:
Solid NaI reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid to form purple fumes of I<sub>2</sub> (g) and hydrogen sulfide gas, H<sub>2</sub>S (g). However, when solid NaCl reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid, the only gas produced is HCl (g).

Explain this difference in the reactions. Your answer should state the role of the sulfuric acid in each reaction.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The difference in the reactions is:
> 
> - Sulfuric acid acts as an acid / proton donor with NaCl
> **OR**
> NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NaHSO<sub>4</sub> + HCl
> **OR**
> 2NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2HCl **[1 mark]**
> - Sulfuric acid acts as an oxidising agent with NaI / I<sup>-</sup>
> **OR**
> NaI is a reducing agent **[1 mark]**
> - I<sup>-</sup> is a more powerful reducing agent than Cl<sup>-</sup>
> **OR**
> Sulfuric acid can oxidise I<sup>-</sup> but not Cl<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The only reaction between NaCl and concentrated sulfuric acid is acid-base: sulfuric acid donates a proton to produce HCl gas. Chloride ions are not strong enough reducing agents to reduce the sulfur in sulfuric acid.
> 
> As you go down Group 17, the halide ions become stronger reducing agents. Iodide ions can reduce the sulfur in sulfuric acid all the way from +6 to -2, producing H<sub>2</sub>S gas along with I<sub>2</sub> and S.

parts.problem_md:
Chlorine is used in water purification. It reacts with water to produce a mixture of acids, one of which is chloric(I) acid, HClO.

i) Explain what is meant by the term oxidising agent in terms of electron transfer.

[1]

ii) Construct an equation for this reaction of chlorine with water.

[1]

iii) Construct an equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide.

Use oxidation numbers to explain why this is a disproportionation reaction.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) An oxidising agent is a species that:
> 
> - Gains electrons / accepts electrons / is an electron acceptor **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction of chlorine with water is:
> 
> - Cl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → HCl + HClO **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The equation for the reaction of chlorine with hot aqueous sodium hydroxide is:
> 
> - 3Cl<sub>2</sub> + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O **[1 mark]**
> 
> This is a disproportionation reaction because:
> 
> - The oxidation number of chlorine changes from 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) to -1 (in NaCl) AND to +5 (in NaClO<sub>3</sub>), showing chlorine is simultaneously oxidised and reduced **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you know the definitions for both oxidising agent (gains electrons / electron acceptor) and reducing agent (loses electrons / electron donor) in terms of electron transfer.
> 
> You should know the equations for the reaction of chlorine with both hot and cold sodium hydroxide:
> 
> - Hot: 3Cl<sub>2</sub> + 6NaOH → 5NaCl + NaClO<sub>3</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O
> - Cold: Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H<sub>2</sub>O
> 
> Both are disproportionation reactions because chlorine is simultaneously oxidised and reduced. If the oxidation number increases, oxidation has occurred; if it decreases, reduction has occurred.
> 
> To verify the oxidation state of Cl in NaClO<sub>3</sub>: Na = +1, each O = -2 (three O atoms = -6), the compound is neutral overall, so Cl must be +5.
